Baby & Child

When Do Babies Start Walking? Timeline and What Helps

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Most babies start walking around 12 months, and anywhere from about 9 to 18 months is within the typical range. First steps usually arrive after months of pulling up, cruising along furniture, and standing alone. If your baby is on the later end of that range, that alone is rarely a cause for concern. Here is what the path to walking usually looks like, how to encourage it safely, and the specific signs that deserve a clinician's opinion.

The typical timeline, and why it is so wide

Most babies take their first independent steps around 12 months, but the full normal range is wide. Some confident babies walk at 9 or 10 months. Others are steady, healthy, and simply not ready until 16, 17, or even 18 months. Walking age says very little about intelligence or future athletic ability. It reflects temperament, body build, opportunity to practice, and where a baby is putting their energy right now. A baby who is busy babbling or perfecting fine motor skills may walk later than one who is focused on movement. If your baby was born early, count from the due date rather than the birth date when you think about milestones.

Try not to measure your baby against a cousin or a neighbor's child. Siblings in the same family often walk months apart. What matters more than the exact date is steady progress: a baby who keeps gaining skills over time is usually on track, even if each stage arrives later than a friend's baby. Healthy children spread across a range, the same way they do on growth charts. Keep an eye on the overall direction, note new skills when they appear, and bring that list to routine checkups so your clinician can see the pattern rather than a single snapshot.

The usual sequence: pulling up, cruising, standing, stepping

Walking almost never appears out of nowhere. Most babies move through a recognizable sequence. First they pull to stand, gripping a sofa, a crib rail, or your pant leg. Then comes cruising: stepping sideways while holding onto furniture for balance. After that, many babies learn to stand alone for a few seconds, often looking surprised about it. Independent steps usually follow standing alone, and the earliest attempts look more like controlled falling than walking. Each stage builds the strength and balance needed for the next one. The ages vary widely, so focus on the order of skills rather than the calendar. A baby working through this chain is making progress even before the first true step.

The gap between cruising and independent walking is often longer than parents expect. Some babies let go of the couch within a couple of weeks. Many others cruise for two or three months before trusting their own balance, and that is still typical. It is also normal for a new walker to drop back to crawling when they want to move fast, and for progress to pause during illness, teething, or a busy stretch like a language burst. Falls come with the territory, which is why a padded, supervised space matters more than perfect technique. Skipping a stage happens too: some babies barely crawl and go straight to pulling up and cruising.

How to encourage first steps safely

The best walking practice is unglamorous: time on the floor with room to move. Clear a safe space, pad sharp corners, and let your baby pull up, squat, fall on a padded bottom, and try again. Limit long stretches in seats, bouncers, and carriers during awake time, since babies build leg and core strength by moving freely. Place a favorite toy on a low, sturdy table to invite pulling up and cruising. Kneel a short distance away and hold out your hands. Cheer the attempts, not just the successes. Practice works best in small, frequent doses when your baby is fed and rested, not as a drill.

A stable push toy, such as a weighted push cart or wagon, can help a cruiser practice stepping forward while holding on. Use it with close supervision: these toys can speed up on hard floors, and stairs need to be gated. Choose one that does not tip when your baby pulls up on it. Indoors, barefoot is best. Bare feet grip the floor, spread for balance, and give the brain useful feedback about weight and position. Non-slip socks work on cold or slippery floors. Save shoes for protection outside, and pick lightweight, flexible soles that let the foot bend rather than stiff or built-up designs.

Why wheeled baby walkers are not recommended

Wheeled baby walkers, the seats on wheels that a baby sits inside and scoots around in, are not recommended. Pediatric safety groups have warned about them for years, and some countries restrict or ban their sale. The problem is speed and reach. A baby in a walker can cross a room in seconds and get to stairs, stoves, cords, and pools faster than an adult can respond. Walkers also raise a baby's height, putting hot drinks and sharp objects within grabbing distance, and they can tip on uneven surfaces or doorway thresholds. Many walker injuries happen while an adult is nearby, simply because the walker moves faster than a caregiver can react.

Walkers also do not do the job their name promises. They hold a baby upright in a position that skips the hard work of balancing, and babies often push along on their toes inside them, which is not the movement pattern real walking needs. Pediatric guidance is consistent that walkers do not speed up walking and may even slow the practice that matters. If you need a safe place to set your baby down, a stationary activity center, a playpen, or a well-gated room does the same job without the wheels. Plain floor time is better still. Nothing about a wheeled walker is required for normal development, so it is fine to skip it entirely.

When to check in with a clinician

Bring it up with your pediatrician or health visitor if your baby is not walking by 18 months. Also mention persistent tiptoe walking, especially if your baby rarely puts their heels down after months of practice, and any clear asymmetry, such as always dragging one leg, strongly favoring one side, or one arm and leg doing far more work than the other. The most important sign at any age is losing skills: a baby who could stand or cruise and then stops deserves a prompt appointment rather than a wait-and-see approach. None of these signs means something is wrong on its own. They simply mean a trained set of eyes should take a look.

At the visit, the clinician will usually watch your baby move, check muscle tone and strength, review the birth history, and ask which skills came when. Sometimes the answer is reassurance and a recheck in a few months. Sometimes it is a referral for physical therapy or an early intervention program, and that kind of support tends to work best when it starts early. Come prepared: jot down dates, questions, and a short video of how your baby moves, in BeMama or wherever you keep notes. A guide like this covers what is typical, but your clinician knows your child. If your gut says something is off, that alone is a good enough reason to ask.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC milestones describe skills that most children can do by a particular age across social, language, thinking, and movement domains. They support observation and conversation but do not replace standardized developmental screening.

Individual skills vary, but caregiver concern matters. Missing several expected skills, losing a skill, or a difference in movement, communication, hearing, or vision should be discussed promptly.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to preserve dated observations, growth, activities, and questions for well-child visits. It cannot label development as normal or delayed.

When to seek help

Contact your child’s healthcare professional whenever you are concerned or notice loss of a skill. Seek urgent care for an acute change, breathing difficulty, loss of responsiveness, or seizure-like activity.

Key takeaways

  • Most babies start walking around 12 months, and about 9 to 18 months is the typical range.
  • The usual path is pulling up, then cruising, then standing alone, then first steps.
  • Cruising can last anywhere from a couple of weeks to a few months before independent walking.
  • Floor time, supervised push toys, and barefoot practice help; wheeled baby walkers are unsafe and do not help.
  • See a clinician for no walking by 18 months, persistent tiptoe walking, strong one-sidedness, or lost skills.

Frequently asked questions

When do babies start walking?

Most babies start walking around 12 months, and the typical range runs from about 9 to 18 months. Early or late within that window says little about long-term ability. Babies born prematurely often walk later, so count from the due date rather than the birth date. Steady progress through pulling up, cruising, and standing alone matters more than the exact date.

My baby is a late walker. When should I worry?

Talk to a clinician if your baby is not walking by 18 months. Also ask about persistent tiptoe walking, a strong preference for one side of the body, or any loss of skills your baby once had. Most late walkers turn out to be developing normally, but those specific signs deserve a proper check rather than online reassurance.

How long does it take to go from cruising to walking?

Cruising to independent walking usually takes anywhere from a few weeks to a few months. Some babies let go of the furniture within a couple of weeks, while others hold on for two or three months, and both patterns are typical. Barefoot practice, plenty of floor time, and a stable push toy used with supervision can help your baby build the confidence to let go.

Do baby walkers with wheels help babies walk sooner?

No. Wheeled walkers do not teach walking and may even slow the practice babies need, because they hold a child upright and skip the balancing work. They are also a safety hazard around stairs, stoves, and pools, which is why pediatric groups recommend against them. A stationary activity center or simple floor time is a safer choice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
